fields.description:
Each tool shares through a local bare repository in the scratch root, as its docs prescribe: bead publishes every write; bd runs `bd dolt push` to refs/dolt/data; br exports, commits .beads/ and pushes. Time a session of agent loops until a second clone sees the work, and record how much the remote grew.

Start-up: the first ready in a new worktree (bead's worktrees share its store, bd's share the main database, br's has no database yet) and in a fresh clone joining the tracker (bead init; bd joining from refs/dolt/data; br importing the clone's JSONL).
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- summary.md gains, per size, the shared session, both start-ups and the remote's growth per 1,000 writes.
- The second clone's answers pass the answer check against the first's.
fields.title: Comparison harness: shared sessions, start-up in a new worktree or clone, remote growth

fields.description:
Two, four and eight agents at once, each tool set up as its docs recommend for several agents: bead in a worktree each; br as that many processes in one checkout; bd in worktrees on its embedded database and, as a variant, in server mode, which needs a dolt binary, pinned and verified like the others. Measure throughput, p50 and p95 per loop and errors by kind (lock timeouts, refusals); afterwards count writes lost and issues two agents both believed they held.

Optionally, a manually triggered CI workflow that runs the two smaller sizes with the pinned tools and uploads summary.md. GitHub's runners are noisy: its figures show trends, not precise ratios.
fields.acceptance_criteria:
- summary.md gains the concurrency table for two, four and eight agents, per tool.
- Each run's check counts lost writes and issues claimed twice.
fields.title: Comparison harness: concurrent agents, bd's server mode, an optional CI job

data.text: Progress (br-edges): 5c079d3 pins what every issue's edges answer on 9cbd60a's code (projection/tests/edges.rs: edges, tags and metadata in order, readiness, blockers, parents, children, dependents, cycles, ready, details, export; digests per seed of every batch of the plain, flawed, awaiting and delivery-order histories; three bead-built journals in full, one new with seven kinds, imported metadata, a merged cycle, concurrent and re-added edges). d073dea extends the differential generator (projection/tests/edges/drawn.rs) with targets naming no issue, new kinds, imports with metadata, concurrent and re-added edges, edges to renamed copies, and read_back compares each edge's metadata. Next: the typed representation. Design: Edge { to: Target (Id(EventId) when the text is an id's spelling, else Text), kind: Arc<str> interned via the codec's name table }; the state part keeps each edge's addition ids, the metadata goes in a section appended to the issue's text record; an op that changes an issue's edges (dep_add, dep_remove, a create binding awaited entries in another issue) needs its texts read in, or extension declines.

Shared code beyond the texts mechanism (br-edges, for the orchestrator to relay to br-ownership): with each edge addition's metadata in the issue's texts, an edge change needs the issue's texts read in. dep_add and dep_remove are about their issue, which stores already read in; but a create whose key an import of another issue waits for makes an edge in that other issue (replay::apply::create::bind), which no record names. I am adding Projection::about(&records) in beadroll-core: the issues records name, plus those waiting by an imported dependency for a key a create among them brings. The store's projection::about (beadroll-store/src/projection.rs, current) and the transaction's (beadroll-sync/src/tx.rs, Emitter::state) call it instead of reading each record's issue themselves; Projection::extend declines when such an issue's texts are not in, as it does for long fields. No other change to how texts are read or written. br-ownership: if your history moves need a wider 'about', add to that function rather than the two callers. Orchestrator: tx.rs's change is in Emitter::state only, not finish/publish_soon.

Step 1 committed (4a119c0, green on 9cbd60a's code): projection::tests::owned pins every issue's claim, generation, claim_history, provisional, lost, stale, detail and export, line by line on three bead-built journals (golden, fleet, a two-machine ownership store with a planted lost claim) and by digest on every differential/delivery-order history plus an ownership-heavy world of its own; commands::ownership pins the end-to-end transcript (every write's answer; show/export/claims/prime/list/ready/blocked human and --json on two machines). Readers found: no command prints claim_history; only commands::ended_by (close/delete/update decisions, on states whose texts are not read in: plan.left subtrees, every target) reads its last entry's ended_by and how; transition::superseded reads stale ends from view_outline after a publish; show/claim/takeover/update details print lost_claims and stale (texts read in by view_of). Replay's claim code only appends. Plan: Stored keeps the last ended claim's (ended_by, how) unread; superseded reads in the texts of the issues its close named; extend's texts_in counts claim/release/close/reopen/delete as touching texts (declines when There), and replay marks texts changed (Read->Here) only when it appends to the history.

fields.acceptance_criteria:
- A write on a tracker with no remote, not --offline, keeps its transaction to the end of the process, as an offline write does; a run that does not end with it frees it as before (cli::ending tests that fail on the base).
- A remote that cannot be chosen keeps the transaction too, and the run reports it where and as a failed publish did ("recorded locally, not yet published (CODE)").
- --offline, writes published at once, claim, release, takeover, update --claim and init behave as before; output and exit codes unchanged.
- Before and after figures: cargo xtask timing --read N on a tracker with no remote (no_remote_write_seconds) at 20,000 and 200,000 events, and the heap peak of such a write (cargo xtask bead).
- docs/REVIEWING.md section 2, docs/GUARANTEES.md, docs/FINDINGS.md X17 and CHANGELOG updated; the stress baseline green.

data.text: Implemented on branch no-remote-write-keeps-transaction: beadroll_sync::destination chooses where a write goes (None when --offline, no remote, or a remote with no URL; the endpoint or the error choosing it otherwise) and publish_soon_at publishes to it; publish_soon is the two together. cli::finish chooses the destination before ended_with and frees the transaction first only for Some(Ok(_)), so a write on a tracker with no remote keeps it to the end of the process, and a remote that cannot be chosen keeps it and is reported as before. Figures (release, fastest of three alternated rounds of five, machine shared with three agents' builds): cargo xtask timing --read 200000, no_remote_write_seconds 0.264 -> 0.174 s (an offline write after a read: 0.174 s); at 20,000 35.6 -> 32.0 ms. Heap peak of a comment on 20,000 imported issues with no remote: 80.64 MB before and after (cargo xtask bead). Left as is: a close or delete that ends a claim still frees its transaction before its own publish on such a tracker, since it reads the store after to answer (superseded).

data.text:
Design (br-copy, roll-lqjj.44 and .45; steps 4 and 5 of roll-lqjj.36, X17): a write-back that copies the bytes of what the write did not touch, then one that appends what changed. Nothing implemented yet; waiting for go.

HOW IT WAS MEASURED. fd5ae9b, release, on the shared 64-core machine (load 3-4 from other agents), so absolute figures are inflated; only runs made together are compared. In process: a scratch probe, not committed: a copy of fd5ae9b (git archive) whose Projection::encode_with is copied into an encode_phases that times each phase and records each issue's and each event record's offset (the issues loop of write_state split from the rest, write_events split into the records and the machines), driven from timing --decode's history (PHASES=1 cargo xtask timing --decode N [--ownership]), best of 5 per phase; assembling, summing and writing timed on the bytes encode gave, as file::bytes and write_cache_parts do them (a Vec of header + parts, sum() of each part, write + rename in target/, not fsynced). End to end: the committed cargo xtask timing --read N and --sync N, three runs each, best kept. Heap: cargo xtask bead (a wrapper as BEAD_UNDER_TEST) on the store timing --read builds. If the step lands I will put the phase split into timing --decode for the PR (copied vs fresh encode), so that its figures come from a committed probe.

1. WHERE A WRITE-BACK'S TIME GOES (fd5ae9b, 200,000 events)
Plain: 19,939 issues, 88,152 events known (all named), 200,000 ids. Ownership-heavy (fd5ae9b, before PR #33): 14,578 issues, 51,594 known.
| phase | made by project() | decoded + 1 comment | compacting (decoded + 1) | ownership, decoded + 1 |
| texts (Here issues' texts) | 33.1 ms, 3.62 MB | 0.19 ms, 2 KB | 0.19 ms | 0.16 ms |
| named | - | - | 18.9 ms | (16.1 compacting) |
| kept (Knowledge::kept) | - | - | 26.3 ms | (13.9 compacting) |
| issues (write_issue x every issue) | 36.4 ms, 7.18 MB (360 B an issue) | 20.7 ms, 7.18 MB | 21.3 ms | 33.3 ms, 8.33 MB (572 B an issue) |
| state rest (by_key, renames, integrity, pending, counters, last_by_thread) | 0.94 ms, 0.51 MB | 0.80 ms | 0.83 ms | 0.33 ms, 0.37 MB |
| asked() + writers + chain breaks | 2.4 ms, 3 KB | 2.5 ms | 2.6 ms | 1.7 ms |
| event records (id, deps, machine, actor) | 21.0 ms, 3.31 MB (37.6 B an event) | 15.2 ms, 3.31 MB | 15.8 ms | 8.1 ms, 2.88 MB (55.9 B) |
| applicable + ancestry (places, clocks, sets, arena) | 2.3 ms, 2.24 MB | 2.3 ms | 2.3 ms | 1.8 ms, 1.78 MB |
| heads + ids | 0.74 ms, 3.20 MB | 1.8 ms | 2.0 ms | 2.7 ms, 3.20 MB |
| index rest (lengths, lasts, superseded, open) | 0.003 ms | 0.004 ms | 0.004 ms | 1.0 ms, 0.72 MB (superseded) |
| encode, whole | 98 ms | 43.4 ms | ~90 ms | 45.6 ms |
| sum state + index (16.4 MB) | | 6.4 ms | | 6.8 ms |
| assemble into one Vec (file::bytes) | | 1.8 ms | | 2.0 ms |
| write + rename 16.4 MB | | 5.1 ms | | 4.9 ms |
| Projection::decode / decode_state | 124 / 59 ms | | | 100 / 54 ms |
| texts read in + extend by one comment | 0.25 ms | | | 0.19 ms |
Parts at 200,000 (plain): state 7.69 MB (issues 7.18, the rest 0.51), index 8.75 MB (event records 3.31, ancestry 2.24, ids 3.20), texts file 3.62 MB; the file 16.46 MB. Names: 21 in the state part, 6 in the index; shared values 6-12 and 6 (the synthetic histories have few writers; a real tracker has one actor per agent thread). At 20,000 (plain, 1,990 issues, 8,850 known): decoded + 1 encodes in 2.8 ms (issues 1.3, event records 0.8, ancestry 0.3, ids 0.2, writers 0.2), sums 0.6 ms, write 0.5 ms; parts 0.77 / 0.83 MB.
The copy step 4 would do instead, simulated on the same bytes (each issue's range and each event record's range copied by offset into a new Vec, with a u32 offset table): issues 0.37 ms, event records 0.39 ms at 200,000 plain; 0.79 and 0.27 ms ownership-heavy.
End to end (timing --read, best of three runs, fd5ae9b): 200,000: list 0.090 s, show 0.082 s, write after a read 0.156 s, read after a write 0.193 s, write after a write 0.152 s; 20,000: 13.5, 12.9, 29.6, 23.4, 29.5 ms. timing --sync 200000 (one run): a sync after a local write 0.281 s, a write published at once 0.528 s.
So a read after a write at 200,000 pays about 110 ms over a plain read: the index decode (~65 ms: Projection::decode 124 against decode_state 59), the encode (43 ms), sums, assembling and writing (13 ms). X17's 94 ms encode (ec773f9) is 43 ms now: step 3 took the compaction out (45 ms), and an issue whose texts are only in the file (its Stored cloned) encodes in about 1.0 us where one whose texts are Here (a fresh projection) takes 1.8 us (summary() computed). Of the 43 ms, 36 ms are the issues and the event records: what step 4 copies.

2. WHAT AN ISSUE'S AND AN EVENT RECORD'S BYTES DEPEND ON OUTSIDE THEM TODAY
- Writer::name: the state part's names (an issue's origin machine, its claim's owner, machine, agent, thread and mode, offline claimants, edge kinds, the ended-by of Stored.ended after #33, the writers' machines) are written inline the first time and as number + 1 after, in one table for the whole part; the index's (event records' machines) likewise. An issue's bytes refer to names an earlier issue defined: re-encoding one issue renumbers every later one.
- Writer::shared: the same for shared values (actors, places, where_, closed_on, claim and offline places), keyed by the Arc's address, not its content: two equal values held by different Arcs are two entries, and the numbers depend on which Arcs the issues hold.
- Text places: an issue's record holds its texts' place (at, len, sum) in the text file, given by encode for texts Here (written anew), and Stored (tags, disputed, ended) recomputed by summary() for texts Read. A record depends on the text file's offsets and generation.
- The writers section depends on every issue's registers (asked(): the events behind registers with several entries, over all issues) and is filtered over every event the knowledge holds: O(issues + events) at every write-back, whatever changed.
- by_key is written beside the issues though it is the issues' keys in issue order (create inserts both; nothing else touches it): 0.5 MB and 0.8 ms of every write-back.
- Event records: the machine and actor through the index's tables. Their place and clock are not in the record but in the ancestry's arrays, indexed by the event's position; clocks point into the shared positions arena and the sets.
- Derived on decode, never written: labels, children, awaiting (finish() in read_state), so relabelling and the parent-child index change no bytes.
- Order: an issue's place in the IndexMap (creation order), an event's in the knowledge (journal order, its index the ancestry's).
WHAT PR #33 CHANGES (read on ownership-history-with-texts, 337b752, not yet restacked onto fd5ae9b): the ended claims, lost claims and stale ends leave write_issue/read_issue for the texts (write_history in write_texts, its own Writer, so self-contained as all texts are); the issue keeps its current claim, generation and offline claims, and Stored gains ended (who ended the last claim, a name, and how). Claims, releases, closes and reopens now need the issue's texts read in (texts_in: needs, not changes) and mark them changed only when the history grows: Issue::ended/lost/ignored call history_changed(), Read -> Here. That is the mark pattern step 4 generalises, and it moves the ownership-heavy history's bytes (8.33 MB of issues at 200,000) out of what step 4 copies. It adds a name to each issue record (ended.by) and leaves the layout's dependencies as above.

3. EVERY PATH THAT CHANGES AN ISSUE OR AN EVENT RECORD BETWEEN A DECODE AND AN ENCODE, AND ITS MARK
Every encode is the store's save, in current(), after decode -> set_texts_file -> about/read_texts -> extend -> save (or after project()); Tx's own extensions and a merge's go through current() or are never encoded. Within that:
a. apply_one on the event's issue: updated_at (unless imported), where_; then the operation: set (registers, stamps own_*), claim/release/close/delete/reopen (claim, generation, offline claims, status and assignee registers, closed_on, extra for a delete, the history: texts after #33), comment (comments: texts; comment_count: global), dep_add/dep_remove (dep_tags, retracted; awaiting.retract takes the issue's own dangling entries), labels (label_tags). Mark: through the issue accessor (below). Also orphans, last_by_thread, comment_count: globals, re-encoded.
b. A create: the new issue (appended: beyond what is stored), by_key, renames (a copy renamed), and each issue awaiting its key (awaiting.arrived, then bind on another issue: dep_tags, dangling taken out). Mark: the accessor (create.rs takes st.issues.get_mut for the other issue).
c. finish_some: settle_awaiting (dangling lists made whole on the issues taken from: already marked by b or a), relabel (labels: derived, no bytes), index_children (derived).
d. Texts: texts_in sets Read -> Here for issues an event changes the texts of (and, after #33, history_changed does when an ownership event grows the history); a Here issue gets a new place at encode. Mark: encode treats every issue with Texts::Here as changed, whatever its marks: a new place is a new record.
e. Texts read in (State::read_texts, by the store's read_texts and about): There -> Read(place), the registers reordered as the texts were written. The record is unchanged if summary(issue, place) == the stored Stored and the non-text registers keep their order. This path must not mark (a show or an export reads in every text), so it alone takes a non-marking accessor, and the tests check its claim byte for byte (5).
f. save's anew path (more of the text file no longer read than read): every text read in, write_texts_anew sets every issue Here: every record changes; a fresh encode.
g. placed() after encode (Here -> Read): after the bytes are written; nothing encodes after.
h. add_unconfirmed (the store's view): after current() returns, never encoded; the accessor marks anyway.
i. Event records: Knowledge::push appends (extend); observe_one records the new event's place and clock and touches only chain_breaks, applicable and the chains' lengths/last (small, re-encoded). An existing event's record (id, deps, machine, actor) and its place and clock never change between compactions: the decoded events are a prefix of the encoded ones. No marks are needed for them, only that prefix property, which the tests check. A compaction (Knowledge::kept, at encode when compaction_due) renumbers everything: the index is encoded fresh then.
j. The rest of the index: heads, lengths, lasts: re-encoded; ids: advance is the only path that adds any (a batch's go in where they sort), and it keeps the list of those it added since the decode, for encode to merge into the stored run: that list is the ids' mark; superseded and open never change in an extension (takeovers and batches that would leave something waiting are declined), so they can be copied.
k. A merge, info, machines: current() with Want::Projection: the same paths as a, b, d, i. A merge that replays: project(), nothing stored, a fresh encode.
The mark: State's issues become a newtype (Issues) that derefs to the IndexMap for reading and mutates only through methods: get_mut marks the issue's position, values_mut marks all, insert appends (beyond what is stored), read_in (for State::read_texts alone) does not mark. A missed mark then needs a mutable path that does not go through Issues, which the compiler refuses, or a misused read_in; encode adds "Texts::Here is changed". The marks are a bitset over the positions the stored bytes hold, cleared at the end of decode (read_state's finish relabels every issue through values_mut). A wrong mark costs a copy; a missed one copies stale bytes, which the next decode reads as current: hence the oracle in 5 on every path.

4. THE LAYOUT (step 4; one projection::ENCODING bump, the store's file layout unchanged: one file, made + state + index, renamed whole)
State part (what decode_state reads): (1) its table: names (count, texts) and shared values (count, values), each entry referred to by its number alone, never defined inline; (2) prefix, name; (3) the issues, each record self-contained but for table numbers and its texts' place: as today's write_issue (after #33) plus the writers of its registers with several entries (event id, machine, actor), which replaces the global writers section and asked() (every writer is the issue's own event: a register holds only events applied to its issue); a state read alone then lists its writers (State::events, State::holds) in issue order, not the journal's, which no command asks and known.rs compares as a set; (4) renames, integrity, pending, orphans, comment_count, last_by_thread, chain breaks (small, re-encoded each time). by_key is not written: decode makes it from the issues, as it makes awaiting.
Index part (what Projection::decode reads after it): (1) its table: names and shared values, and the ancestry's chain sets and positions arena, all append-only between compactions; (2) the event records, each: id, deps, machine, actor, place, clock (set, arena start): everything per event in one record, the ancestry's per-event arrays gone; (3) machines, applicable, the chains' sequenced/lengths/last, compacted, heads, ids (one ascending run), lengths, lasts, superseded, open.
No offset table is stored: decode reads the records in order and records where each issue began (a Vec<u32>, 80 KB at 200,000), and where the event records, sets and arena end. A stored table would be bytes to validate and nothing more in step 4; step 5's root gets one.
What decode keeps to copy from: the parts as read (the store moves its Encoded into Projection::decode, held as an Arc so a clone shares it), the issue offsets, the table sizes. Cost: the 16.4 MB the store read are held from the decode to the write-back instead of freed after it, at 200,000 (1.6 MB at 20,000). The store lets go of them when current() returns (a write keeps its transaction to exit, not the bytes). At the write-back, today's peak (projection + new parts + the assembled copy file::bytes makes) becomes projection + kept + new parts once file::bytes writes the header and parts through write_cache_parts as parts (it takes a list already): the same peak. Measured on fd5ae9b at 200,000 (cargo xtask bead, on the timing --read store): a list 51 MB, a write 88 MB, the read after a write, which writes back, 103 MB (118 MB the first time after a sync). Prediction for step 4: the list and the write unchanged (decode_state keeps nothing; a write lets go of the bytes before its transaction starts), the write-back within its Vecs' slack of 103 MB (today the parts grow by doubling; a copying encode knows their sizes and reserves them); measured in the PR, not assumed.
Encode, when there is something to copy from: the state table written whole (the stored entries, then those this write-back added); every stored issue unmarked and not Here copied from its range; every other issue written against the table (names looked up by content, values by address first and then by content, so a value equal to a stored one does not get a second entry); the rest written. The index, when it does not compact: the table, sets and arena as stored plus what was added; the stored event records copied as one range plus the new ones written; ids merged as ranges of the stored run between the batch's ids (16 bytes each, fixed width: no per-id work); the rest written. A fresh encode (everything written, the tables made anew from what is referenced) when there is nothing stored (project()), when the knowledge compacts (index only: event records are renumbered), when every text is written anew (state part), or when the state table holds more than an eighth more entries than when it was last made fresh (a count in the state part; the index's table is bounded by its compaction).
Expected encode at 200,000: copies ~0.8 ms + the issues and events marked + the small rest (~1-2 ms) = about 2-3 ms where it is 43 ms; leaving the writers, by_key and the ancestry out of it would leave about 8 ms.
decode_state: the same work in a different order (the table read before the issues instead of inline; a number per reference as now; by_key cloned from the issue's key instead of read: one String either way); it must not be slower, and timing --decode will say so.

5. HOW THE TESTS SEE A MISSED MARK, BEFORE ANYTHING CHANGES
First commit, tests only, green on main once #33 is on it (the layout the step builds on): projection/tests/marked.rs.
- record_of(issue): the issue's record written alone, with a fresh Writer (names and values inline: deterministic by content), its texts' place as encode would write it (a Here issue a place no record has).
- At every read_back (the decode the differential tracks take, and the deferred track's), the baseline: every issue's record_of by position, and the decoded knowledge's event records (id, deps, machine, actor, place, clock) by position.
- After every extension (each track, the deferred track, the flawed histories), changed(baseline, projection): the issues at stored positions whose record_of differs, and whether any baseline event record differs or moved. Checks: changed issues are among the marked ones, and no baseline event record changed unless the knowledge was compacted since. On today's code marked() is every issue (today's encode writes them all, which is the honest mark of the code as it is), so the check passes; the step's code replaces it with the projection's own marks, and then it bites.
- A tally of what changed and how, with minima the generator must reach (enough()): issues changed as the event's own issue, by a set, an ownership event, a delete, a comment, an edge; another issue bound by a create's key; a copy renamed; texts re-placed; an issue only read in and unchanged (path e); event records appended between compactions and rewritten by one. Where a path is drawn too rarely, the draw code gets a function of its own (the edges' drawn.rs is the model), with the generator-only commit first and every pinned answer re-made on it if the histories change.
- Self-tests: changing one field of one issue, or an event's record, is seen.
Second commit (marks, no layout change): Issues and its marks; marked() becomes the projection's. A tightness check too: an issue only read in is not marked (so a read that reads every text does not quietly re-encode everything).
Layout and copy commits: read_back also encodes fresh (encode_with a test-only "copy nothing") and asserts that both decode alike and that each issue the encode copied has the bytes write_issue gives it now against the same table, naming the seed, batch and issue otherwise.
Mutations I will show failing, each with the test that fails:
1. apply_one's updated_at through the non-marking accessor (an issue changed, unmarked).
2. create.rs's bind on an awaited issue through it (another issue changed, unmarked).
3. An event record changed: an existing event's actor rewritten in extend; and a push before the end.
4. A stale name number: the seeded name map off by one.
5. A stale shared-value number: the address map off by one, and the content lookup dropped (a value appended twice).
6. The offsets off by one record (issue i copied from i+1's start).
7. Texts Here copied (the Here rule dropped).
8. A compaction that copies the event records anyway.
9. An id of the batch left out of the merged run.
10. The state table never made fresh (a bound on its entries fails: a test with many distinct actors).
11. read_texts marking (the tightness check fails: a speed-up lost, not an answer).
12. by_key made from the issues in another order, or a renamed copy's key left out.
Plus the existing differential, flawed, deferred and many_seeds runs, each comparing with replay after every write-back.

6. STEP 5 ON THIS LAYOUT (roll-lqjj.45)
Files: <store>/projection becomes the root, still renamed whole (write_cache_parts); the records go to <store>/projection-records, append-only like the text file: a header (magic, generation: the sum of the bytes it was started with), appended under its own lock at its length, started again (renamed whole) when it holds more bytes no longer placed than an eighth of those placed (tighter than the text file's "more than read, plus 1 MiB", because every decode, a list's included, reads and sums the live records), and at a compaction of the knowledge or a fresh state table, which rewrite most records anyway. Texts stay in their own file: a list never reads them.
What goes in the records file: a start-again lays the base out in kind order, the state half first (state table, issue records) and the index half after (index table, sets, arena, event records, ids); each write-back then appends one extent, its own state half (the state table's added entries, the issue records written: marked, Here, new) and index half (the index table's added entries, sets and arena positions, the new event records, the batch's ids as an ascending run), each half placed and summed apart by the root. Weighed and not chosen: the records in the text file itself (one file, one lock, one argument), since a list would then read past texts it never prints.
The root: header and sums as now; made (build, journal files, the text file's generation and the records file's); the state's small rest (prefix, name, renames, integrity, pending, counters, last_by_thread, chain breaks); the issue table (each issue's offset and length in the records file, in issue order: ~8 B an issue, 160 KB at 200,000); every live extent (at, len, sum, kind); the index's small rest (machines, applicable, chains, compacted, heads, lengths, lasts, superseded, open). About 0.2-0.3 MB at 200,000 where the file is 16.4 MB (X17's ~1 MB assumed the ancestry and by_key stayed in it).
Reading: decode_state reads the root, then the base's state half and the appended tail (two reads, not a read an extent), sums the state halves, and parses the issue records at the root's offsets; Projection::decode reads and sums the index halves too, the id runs merged (concatenated, sorted, refused if not distinct). Decode keeps nothing of the bytes: an untouched record stays where it is, so step 4's held copy goes and so does the write-back's new 16 MB.
The durability argument (REVIEWING section 2, roll-lqjj.27) must then cover a third file, needed by every decode where texts are needed only by some commands:
- Interrupted between the append and the root's rename (failpoint projection.records-appended, and atomic-write on the root): the old root stands; the appended bytes are unplaced, garbage the next append goes after (always at the file's length) and the rule above counts.
- Two processes writing back at once: appends are serialized by the records file's lock, held through the root's rename as save holds the text file's now (the text file's lock taken first, always, so two savers cannot deadlock), so a root names only extents written before it, its own included; the last rename wins and the other's extents are garbage. A process whose lock outlived a start-again appended to the unlinked file: its root names the old generation and is refused, a replay.
- A root whose sums do not match: no projection, as now. A root whose sums match but whose extents a crash lost, zeroed or cut (the rename reached the disk before the append did): an extent's sum fails, so the decode fails and the journal is replayed; unlike a text, a record is needed by every command, so it costs a replay at the next command rather than at the next command that prints the text. A records file of another generation: the same.
- Readers against writers: a reader takes only what the root it read places, all of it written before that root, never rewritten (appends only); a start-again between its root and its open shows another generation: a replay, rarely.
- The text file's argument is unchanged; the pairings (root newer, older, another generation, one without the other) get the same treatment for the records file, and the tests (projection::tests, the black-box storage::projection with a bead killed between the append and the rename, and every pairing of root, records and text file) must say so.
Should step 4's layout change so that step 5 needs no second change of the records' bytes? Yes, and the layout in 4 is chosen for it: each event record carries its place and clock (else the ancestry's 2.2 MB stay in the root or need their own format change); records refer to tables by absolute number and never define entries inline; nothing in a record is relative to where it sits; writers ride in the issue records and by_key is derived (else they stay in the root). Step 5 then changes the root and where the records sit, not their bytes; one ENCODING bump each.

7. EXPECTED GAINS AND COSTS
Step 4, 200,000 events, plain: a write-back's encode 43 ms -> about 3 ms (8 ms if writers, by_key and the ancestry were left as they are); timing --read: read after a write 0.193 s -> about 0.155 s; write after a read 0.156 s and write after a write 0.152 s unchanged (they do not write back below the 64th; the write that crosses it gains the 40 ms); list, show, ready unchanged (decode_state the same work); --sync: unchanged but for its write-backs (the merge writes back only past the 64th). Ownership-heavy (fd5ae9b): encode 45.6 -> about 5 ms; after #33 the issues are smaller and both figures will be re-measured. 20,000: encode 2.8 -> about 0.5 ms, read after a write 23.4 -> about 21 ms; nothing else moves. Bytes: -0.5 MB (by_key) of 16.4 MB; the tables grow by what write-backs add between fresh encodes, an eighth at most. Heap: +16.4 MB held from decode to write-back at 200,000 (1.6 MB at 20,000), the peak unchanged once the assembled copy goes.
Step 5, 200,000: a write-back writes about 0.3 MB (root) + ~1-2 KB appended instead of 16.4 MB: sums 6.4 -> ~0.2 ms, assembling 1.8 -> 0, writing 5.1 -> ~0.2 ms: about -12 ms (read after a write -> about 0.143 s); 20,000 about -1.1 ms. Reads read and sum up to an eighth more record bytes before a start-again. Heap: step 4's held copy and the write-back's 16.4 MB of new parts go. A start-again of the records file rewrites everything once every (live / 8) / (bytes a write-back appends) write-backs: about 2 MB / 0.5 KB, some thousands at 200,000, besides the ones a knowledge compaction brings.
What X17's design missed or got wrong, now measured:
- The encode is 43 ms on fd5ae9b, not 94: step 3 took 45 ms; the issues are 20.7 ms of a decoded projection (49 was a fresh one, every texts' summary computed), the event records 15.2 ms (not 21). Step 4's gain is ~40 ms, not 50-70.
- Event records need no marks and no offset table: between compactions they are append-only and never change (Knowledge::push), so they are one range copied; at a compaction they are renumbered and written fresh.
- The ancestry (2.2 MB, 2.3 ms) is per event and append-only too: it belongs in the event records, or step 5's root is 2 MB, not 1.
- The writers section and asked() are O(issues + events) at every write-back (2.5 ms), and by_key (0.5 MB, 0.8 ms) is derivable: both go.
- The shared-value table is keyed by the Arc's address: copying needs it content-stable.
- Keeping the stored bytes costs 16.4 MB of heap at 200,000 unless the assembled copy goes; step 5 removes the need.
- Step 5's records file must compact tighter than the text file, because every decode reads it.
- After steps 4 and 5 the read after a write still pays ~65 ms at 200,000 to decode the index and ~0.3 ms to extend: the option X17 rejected, a write writing back its own projection, cost a 106 ms write-back in the write then; after step 4 it costs ~3 ms of encode and 13 ms of sums and writing, ~1 ms of those after step 5, and would make the read after a write a plain read (0.08-0.09 s). I recommend the orchestrator weigh it as a step after 5 (its lock and crash questions are those of a write-back today); I do not plan it in .44 or .45.
Risk: medium-high for step 4 (a missed mark is a stale answer until the next replay; the Issues newtype and the oracle are the defence); high for step 5 (a third file in the crash argument).

What step 5 takes from step 4's design (br-copy, full design on roll-lqjj.44): step 4 makes every issue record and every event record self-contained but for table numbers (the names and shared values, and the ancestry's chain sets and positions arena, in tables of their own, append-only between fresh encodes), puts each event's place and clock in its record, moves the writers into the issue records and derives by_key, so that step 5 changes where the records sit and the root, never the records' bytes. Step 5: <store>/projection becomes a small root renamed whole (made, the state's and index's small rest, the issue table of offsets, every live extent with its sum; about 0.2-0.3 MB at 200,000 events where the file is 16.4 MB on fd5ae9b), and the records go to <store>/projection-records, append-only under its own lock (taken after the text file's, held through the root's rename), one extent per write-back with a state half and an index half summed apart, started again when it holds more bytes no longer placed than an eighth of those placed (tighter than the text file, since every decode reads it). Measured on fd5ae9b at 200,000: summing 6.4 ms, assembling 1.8 ms and writing 5.1 ms of every write-back, about 12 ms of what step 5 removes, and the 16.4 MB step 4 holds to copy from. The durability bullet must then cover a third file needed by every decode: an append without its root (garbage, appended after), two writers (serialized by the lock, last rename wins), a root whose extents a crash lost (a sum fails, a replay at the next command), another generation, and every pairing of root, records and text file, with failpoint and black-box kill tests.

fields.description: Proposed in br-copy's design for roll-lqjj.44 (its comment of 2026-10-17); not planned in .44 or .45. Measured on fd5ae9b at 200,000 events (release, shared machine): a read after a write takes 0.193 s, where a plain read takes 0.082-0.090 s. After X17's steps 4 and 5 it would still pay about 65 ms to decode the index (Projection::decode 124 ms against decode_state 59 ms) and about 0.3 ms to extend, because a write leaves its record for the next command to apply and write back. X17's design (roll-lqjj.36) rejected a write writing back its own projection when a write-back cost 106 ms and the index decode 26 ms. After step 4 a write-back would cost about 3 ms of encode and 13 ms of sums and writing (about 1 ms after step 5), and the index decode is 65 ms since PR #20 moved the event records into the index. Weigh it once roll-lqjj.44 lands, against its measured write-back: what a write gains in time and heap peak, whether it writes back under the store lock or after it as a reader does, how it fits step 1's rule (a write writes back only past a 64th of the projection), and the crash and race argument, which should be a write-back's today.
fields.acceptance_criteria: A decision recorded in docs/REVIEWING.md section 2 with figures: either a write writes back its own projection and the read after a write costs what a plain read costs (measured end to end at 20,000 and 200,000 events), or the reason it does not.
fields.title: Weigh a write writing back its own projection once roll-lqjj.44 makes a write-back cheap
